headline: August 7 and Washington's Already Past Its Prime Window — Time to Adjust
subhead: The wall is still paying off but the pattern's shifting from chunk to troll as tides go soft into next week.
body_markdown:
I've been running this canyon long enough to know the calendar lies to you if you let it. Every other captain on the VHF is talking like mid-August just started the season — for Hudson, for Wilmington, sure. Not here. Washington runs on its own clock because of where it sits relative to the stream, and by the first week of August we're already past the opening act and deep into the second. If you're planning your first trip of the year out here this week thinking you caught the front end of it, you didn't. You caught the middle, which honestly might be the better seat.

We flagged this last week — said the yellowfin would carry the volume on the temperature breaks along the wall, that the billfish presence would build the way it does in early August, and that boats grading their weeks honestly would call it a B-plus: fish in the box every trip, the only knock being consistency trip to trip. That's exactly what's playing out. Nobody's getting skunked out here right now, but nobody's calling their outfitter to brag about a 20-for-20 morning either.

The warm filament that's been sitting on the edge since late July hasn't moved much, which is the whole story. It's held bait and held fish along that break where the canyon wall drops from the 100-fathom curve down toward the 1000, roughly working the stretch from 39°08'N, 72°33'W south through 39°02'N, 72°28'W. That's still the address. Surface temps on the warm side of that break are pushing mid-to-upper 70s, cooling off fast once you slide back over the edge into green water — and that seam is where the yellowfin are stacking up to feed, mixed in with scattered bigeye that are showing better after dark than during the day.

Trolling a standard spread — Green Machines and Zukers in the shotgun, naked ballyhoo and a few skirted horse ballyhoo down the middle — has been the more consistent producer through the daylight hours, and that's going to matter more as we roll into next week. Tides have been softening out of the recent stretch and they're going to keep going that direction, which historically shifts the percentages here away from chunking and toward the troll. If you've been a chunk-and-wait guy on the wall all summer, this is the week to start moving the boat again instead of anchoring up on the drift and hoping the current brings them to you.

That said, chunking bunker and butterfish over the deeper structure — the humps and the drop just north of the main canyon axis — is still putting yellowfin in the box for the boats willing to sit on it, especially in that dawn window before the sun gets high. It's just not the layup it was two weeks ago when the current was still ripping and the bait was pinned tight against the edge.

White marlin have been the pleasant surprise. Numbers aren't huge, but they're building the way they should for this point in the season, and we're seeing them come up on dredge teasers and small blue-and-white islanders worked just off the temperature break rather than deep in the canyon proper. If you've got a pitch bait ready and someone on the bridge with sharp eyes on the temp gauge, you're in decent shape to get a shot or two per trip. Mahi are scattered under whatever weed lines are holding — nothing to write home about in size, mostly schoolies in the 5 to 12 pound range, but they'll fill a cooler slot while you're working bigger fish on the troll. Wahoo have shown up on the high-speed gear worked right on the color change itself, not sitting off it — that's an important distinction this time of year, the wahoo want the edge tighter than the yellowfin do.

We also called the frontal timing right — said the passage would churn things inshore but that the southern canyons, Washington included, take southerly wind better than the New York bight boats do, and that by midweek the window would open back up settled. That's held true. The blow pushed through, kicked up a short-lived chop on the grounds, and by Wednesday it laid back down into the kind of glass we've had most of this week.

Looking ahead, I'd treat this coming week as a transition trip more than a repeat of what worked in July. With the tide continuing to soften, I'd lean harder into the troll pattern early and save the chunk bags for late afternoon into dusk when the current picks back up enough to hold a slick. If that warm filament holds its position along the wall — and there's no strong signal yet that it's sliding — the yellowfin should keep grading out as a B-plus fishery: dependable, not spectacular, worth the run. If it starts sliding east the way these things sometimes do into September, I'd expect the bite to follow it, and boats will need to shift their coordinates east of that 72°28'W line to stay on the fish. For now, that's where I'd put my spread.
